title: The dollar and US rates: why Washington sets India's price tag
hook:
Here's a puzzle that confuses a lot of Indian investors. In 2022 most Indian companies grew their profits at a healthy clip. Banks were lending more, consumers were spending, the economy was among the fastest growing in the world. Yet the price investors were willing to pay for each rupee of those profits fell, and foreign funds sold Indian shares at a record pace.

Nothing had gone wrong in India. What had changed was a number set thousands of miles away: the yield on a ten-year US government bond. It had more than doubled in a matter of months as the Federal Reserve raced to fight inflation. And when that number moves, it reprices almost every asset on the planet, including your Indian stocks.

Why should a bond in Washington decide what a bank share in Mumbai is worth? This chapter walks through the plumbing: what a US yield really is, the three channels through which it reaches India, and why the kind of rise we are seeing now is the kind India likes least.
short: The US ten-year Treasury yield is the world's benchmark safe return. Every investment, including Indian shares, is priced as a premium over it.
India's valuation premium over other emerging markets behaves like a long-dated asset: it shrinks when US real yields rise, even if Indian earnings do not change.
US rates reach India through three channels, fastest first: foreign flows and the rupee, then valuation multiples, then trade, technology budgets and visas.
Why yields rise matters as much as how far. A rise driven by inflation fear and heavy government borrowing, like today's, is worse for India than one driven by strong US growth.
Domestic investors now cushion US shocks far better than in 2013, but they cannot fully offset a strong dollar and a wide external gap at the same time.

sections.heading: Why a bond in Washington sets a price in Mumbai
sections.html:
Start with what a US ten-year Treasury is: a loan to the American government for ten years. Because the US government can always print the dollars it owes, investors treat this as the safest long-term investment in the world. Its yield, the annual return you lock in by buying it today, is the closest thing finance has to a risk-free rate.

Everything else is priced as a premium over that. If a safe US bond pays you little, you are happy to take risks elsewhere for a modest extra return: emerging-market shares, small companies, long-dated growth stories. If the safe bond suddenly pays you a lot, every risky asset has to offer more to compete, and the only way it can do that overnight is by getting cheaper.

This is where India comes in. Indian shares trade at a fat premium to other emerging markets because investors believe Indian companies will keep growing for a very long time. In plain terms, much of what you pay for when you buy the Nifty is profit that will arrive many years from now. And money that arrives far in the future is exactly what a higher interest rate punishes most.

[[fig:1]]

The chart shows the US ten-year since mid-2015. Notice the shape: a long, gentle drift in the late 2010s, a collapse to a record low when Covid hit, then the steepest climb in decades once the Fed started hiking in 2022. The last stretch, during the Iran war, has pushed it to the highest point in our data. The shaded bands mark the episodes that rattled Indian markets, and you can see that several of them coincide with yields jumping.

sections.heading: What is inside a bond yield, and why it matters which part is rising
sections.html:
A bond yield looks like one number, but it is really three stacked on top of each other. Knowing which layer is moving tells you what kind of shock you are dealing with.

  • The real yield. The return investors demand after inflation. It rises when the economy is strong and the central bank is expected to keep rates high. This is the purest measure of how expensive money is.
  • Inflation compensation. The extra return investors want to cover the inflation they expect over the life of the bond. An oil shock pushes this up.
  • The term premium. The extra return for the plain discomfort of locking money away for a long time when the future is uncertain. It rises when investors worry about government debt, heavy bond issuance or unpredictable policy.

Why does this matter for India? Because a yield rising for good reasons, strong American growth, usually comes with strong global demand, which helps Indian exporters and cyclicals. A yield rising for bad reasons, inflation fear and a glut of government bonds, brings the higher discount rate without the growth to compensate.

A US yield rising on growth is a headwind. A yield rising on fear is a tax.

Today's move looks like the second kind. An oil-driven inflation scare has lifted inflation compensation, and heavy US government borrowing has lifted the term premium. History suggests term-premium rises tend to persist rather than reverse quickly, and they tend to come with a strong dollar. For India, that is the uncomfortable combination: dearer global money and a weaker rupee at the same time.

sections.heading: Channel one: the money goes home and the rupee slides
sections.html:
The fastest channel is money itself. A global fund manager deciding how much to put into India is constantly comparing it with what she could earn safely in dollars. When the safe US return rises, the hurdle for owning Indian assets goes up with it. Some of that money simply goes home.

There is a currency twist that makes this worse. A foreign investor earns returns in rupees but counts them in dollars. If the rupee weakens, her Indian gains shrink when converted back. So when US yields rise and the dollar strengthens, she faces a double hit: a better alternative at home and a falling currency in India. Hedging that currency risk costs roughly the gap between Indian and American interest rates, so as US rates climb towards Indian levels, the cushion that made India attractive gets thinner.

The selling then feeds on itself. Foreign funds sell Indian shares, convert rupees into dollars to take the money out, and that conversion pushes the rupee down further. The RBI usually steps in by selling dollars from its reserves to slow the fall, which, as the RBI chapter explains, also drains rupees from the banking system and tightens money at home.

Since 2024 there is a second pipe. Indian government bonds now sit in global bond indices, so index-tracking bond funds hold them automatically. That brought a steadier stream of foreign money, but it also means that when global bond funds cut risk, India's bond market feels it directly, and bond yields at home can rise along with American ones.

sections.heading: Channel two: the multiple shrinks even when profits don't
sections.html:
The second channel is quieter but often bigger. It works through valuation multiples, the price investors pay for each rupee of a company's profit.

Think about what a share really is: a claim on all of a company's future profits. To decide what that is worth today, investors shrink each future year's profit by a discount rate, and the further away the profit, the more it gets shrunk. The discount rate starts from the risk-free rate. So when the US ten-year rises, every future rupee is worth a little less today, and the profits furthest in the future lose the most.

That is why higher US yields hurt different Indian stocks very differently. A cheap, mature company that pays out most of its earnings now, such as a utility or a large public sector firm, barely notices. A richly valued consumer brand, a new-age platform company or a fast-growing financial firm whose value lies mostly in profits a decade out gets hit hard, even if this quarter's results are perfect.

It is the same logic for the market as a whole. India's premium over other emerging markets is a bet on long-lasting growth, which makes the whole index behave like a long-dated asset. Falling US real yields, as in 2020 and 2021, inflate that premium. Rising ones, as in 2022 and again now, deflate it. Nothing about Indian earnings needs to change for the price tag to move.

sections.heading: Channel three: tariffs, tech budgets and visas
sections.html:
The slowest channel runs through the real economy. America is India's largest export market, and the biggest single slice of that is services, above all the IT industry.

Here the effects pull in opposite directions, which is why IT is so hard to call. A strong dollar is good for Indian IT companies in the short run: they earn in dollars and pay most of their staff in rupees, so every dollar of revenue buys more salaries. But high US rates make American companies cautious. Chief financial officers delay big technology projects, banks trim discretionary spending, and Indian IT firms feel it a few quarters later as smaller deals and slower growth.

Then there is policy. In September 2025 Washington announced a one-time fee of a hundred thousand dollars on new applications for the skilled-worker visa Indian IT firms have long relied on to send engineers to client sites. IT shares fell sharply on the next trading day, even after the White House clarified that the fee applied only to new applications. Add the tariffs on Indian goods imposed in 2025, and the trade channel has become as much about politics as about interest rates.

So when you read that US rates are rising, think about IT in layers: a short-term boost from the currency, a medium-term drag from client budgets, and a long-running question mark over visas and tariffs.

sections.heading: What history says, sector by sector
sections.html:
Theory is tidy. Markets are not. So we went back through our own data and looked at every stretch when the US ten-year rose by more than three quarters of a point over a year, and asked how each Indian sector did against the Nifty over three-month windows within those stretches.

[[fig:2]]

Read the bars as performance relative to the Nifty: bars to the right beat the index, bars to the left lagged it. The label next to each bar shows its t-statistic, a measure of how confident we can be that the pattern is real rather than luck. As a rule of thumb, anything smaller than about two and a half is indistinguishable from noise.

Only one sector clears that bar: metals, which beat the index in those windows. But be careful with that result. US yields often rise when the world economy is running hot and commodity prices are climbing, the regime this site calls reflation. Metals are probably riding the commodity cycle rather than the bond yield itself. Energy points the same way, more weakly.

The surprise is IT, which barely moved relative to the market. That fits the layered story above: the weaker rupee in those windows roughly offset the drag from higher rates and cautious clients. Realty and gold lagged, as you would expect when money gets dearer, but not reliably enough to bet on. The broader lesson is humility. US rates set the backdrop, but sector moves depend on why rates are rising.

sections.heading: Why India bends more than it breaks these days
sections.html:
In 2013 a mere hint from the Fed sent the rupee into free fall and got India labelled one of the most fragile economies in the world. In 2022 the Fed raised rates at the fastest pace in four decades, foreign investors sold Indian shares on a record scale, and yet the Nifty ended the year roughly flat while American markets fell hard. What changed?

Mainly, Indian households. Monthly investments into equity mutual funds through systematic plans became a habit for millions of people, and that money keeps coming regardless of what the Fed does. Domestic institutions now routinely buy what foreigners sell. The RBI also built up a much larger pile of foreign exchange reserves after 2013 and has shown it will use them.

But the cushion has limits. India is most vulnerable when its external gap, the current account deficit, is wide, because it then needs foreign money to plug the hole. Oil is the biggest driver of that gap. So the dangerous combination is high US yields together with expensive oil: dearer global money exactly when India needs more of it. That is the combination in front of us now.

history.title: Volcker's Saturday night
history.story:
In October 1979 Paul Volcker, the new Fed chairman, called a rare Saturday evening press conference and announced that the Fed would stop targeting interest rates and squeeze the money supply instead, whatever that did to rates. US inflation was out of control, and Volcker was prepared to cause a recession to kill it. Rates shot to levels America had never seen. Homebuilders mailed him planks of wood to show the houses nobody could afford to build; farmers drove tractors to the Fed's building in protest.

The pain did not stay in America. Latin American governments had borrowed heavily in dollars at floating rates during the 1970s. In August 1982 Mexico's finance minister, Jesús Silva Herzog, flew to Washington to tell officials his country could not pay. Brazil, Argentina and others followed, and the region lost a decade of growth.
history.lesson: When US real rates surge, the countries and companies that borrowed in dollars get hurt first and hardest.

history.title: The great bond massacre
history.story:
In February 1994 Alan Greenspan's Fed raised rates for the first time in five years, by a small amount, and kept going through the year. Bond investors had piled into bets that rates would stay low, and the rise caught them badly wrong. Prices of long bonds collapsed in what Fortune magazine called the great bond massacre.

The casualties were colourful. Robert Citron, the treasurer of wealthy Orange County in California, had borrowed heavily to bet on falling rates; in December the county filed for bankruptcy. Within weeks Mexico, which had attracted a flood of short-term foreign money, was forced to devalue the peso. The tequila crisis needed a rescue organised by the US Treasury under Robert Rubin.
history.lesson: Fast, surprising US hikes break the weakest, most leveraged borrowers first, often thousands of miles from Washington.

history.title: The taper tantrum
history.story:
In May 2013 Ben Bernanke told Congress that the Fed might start slowing its bond buying in the coming meetings. He did not raise rates. He did not even cut the purchases. He merely hinted. Bond yields jumped and money rushed out of emerging markets.

India was among the worst hit because it was running a record current account deficit and high inflation. The rupee crashed to record lows through the summer, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram raised import duties on gold again and again to stem dollar outflows, and families paying children's fees abroad watched the bill balloon. A Morgan Stanley analyst lumped India with Brazil, Indonesia, Turkey and South Africa as the Fragile Five. It took a new governor, Raghuram Rajan, and a special dollar deposit scheme to turn the tide.
history.lesson: India is most exposed to the Fed when its own external gap is wide; a hint can do what a hike does.

history.title: A long way from neutral
history.story:
Through 2018 Jerome Powell's Fed kept raising rates while oil climbed. In October Powell remarked in an interview that rates were still a long way from neutral, the level that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy. Markets heard more hikes ahead, and a global sell-off followed.

India was hit from several sides at once. The rupee slid to record lows, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley cut excise duty on petrol and diesel to soften pump prices, and the default of the infrastructure lender IL&FS froze the market for short-term loans to non-bank lenders. Within days of the new year, Powell signalled the Fed would be patient, and markets recovered.
history.lesson: Slow, steady US hikes hurt India through the currency and through dear oil, not through one dramatic crash.

history.title: Powell's short speech
history.story:
In August 2022, at the central bankers' retreat in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Powell delivered one of the shortest keynote speeches in memory. Its message was blunt: the Fed would keep raising rates to kill inflation, and that would bring some pain to households and businesses. The Dow fell more than a thousand points that afternoon.

The Fed was in the middle of its fastest hiking cycle in four decades, and foreign investors sold Indian shares on a record scale that year. The rupee hit new lows. But something new happened: Indian households kept investing through their monthly mutual fund plans, domestic institutions bought what foreigners sold, and the Nifty ended the year roughly flat.
history.lesson: Domestic flows now soften even severe US shocks, but the rupee still takes the hit.

history.title: Term premium meets oil
history.story:
When the Iran war pushed oil sharply higher in 2026, the US ten-year climbed with it, reaching the highest level in our data in October. This time the driver was not a booming American economy. It was an oil-driven inflation scare layered on top of heavy US government borrowing, the kind of rise that lifts inflation compensation and the term premium rather than the real growth outlook.

For India the timing was awkward. Trade talks with Washington had stalled, new US sanctions on Iranian crude reached two Indian firms, and foreign investors kept selling.
history.lesson: Long yields rising on inflation fear are worse for India than yields rising on growth, because the higher discount rate arrives without the demand to offset it.

What to watch next: whether the US rise is driven by inflation fear or by growth, which oil will largely decide; the Fed's language on future rates; and the dollar. A turn in any of the three would ease the pressure on Indian valuations before it shows up in flows.
sowhat:
While the US ten-year stays near its highs, expect foreign investors to stay underweight India and the most richly valued large caps to feel the pressure first.

  • Most exposed in our industry map are IT and software, through client budgets, visas and tariffs, and asset managers, whose fees depend on equity flows and market levels.
  • Be careful with long-duration growth stocks on rich multiples, where most of the value lies in profits far in the future.
  • Less exposed are cheaper, mature businesses that pay out earnings now and earn them mostly at home.
  • Historically, metals have done best when US yields rose, but that is largely the commodity cycle, not the bond yield, so treat it with caution.

What would flip it: US yields turning down because inflation fear fades, a weaker dollar, or the oil price breaking lower. India's premium tends to re-expand quickly once the global discount rate stops rising.
